axes-points: Every economics graph has two labeled axes, and every point on it is one ordered pair: the horizontal value first, then the vertical value. Points that rise together show a direct relationship; points that move in opposite directions show an inverse one. Label every axis and every curve, with the standard variable on each axis, because that is the first thing a reader checks.
slopes-curves: Slope is rise over run, the change in the vertical value divided by the change in the horizontal value. A line that rises to the right has a positive slope, one that falls has a negative slope, a horizontal line has a slope of zero, and a vertical line keeps the horizontal value fixed. A straight line has the same slope at every point, while a bowed curve changes slope as you move along it.
shifts-movements: Every curve is drawn holding other things equal. A change in a variable on one of the axes moves you along the curve to a new point; a change in anything else shifts the whole curve right or left. On the exam, name the cause, decide shift or movement, draw the new curve with a new subscript and an arrow, and label everything.
curves-crossing: Where two curves cross, they agree on one price and one quantity. When one curve shifts, the crossing slides along the other curve to a new point. Mark both crossings with dashed lines to both axes, label the old and new values, and state the direction of each change: that before-and-after comparison is what readers score on every graph in the course.
scarcity: Scarcity means wants are greater than the resources to meet them, so every person, business and government must choose, and every choice is a trade-off. The resources are the four factors of production: land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship. A society's economic system, market, command or mixed, decides what to produce, how to produce it and for whom; most real economies mix markets with some government roles.
opportunity-cost-ppc: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative you give up, and the production possibilities curve shows it for a whole economy: every point on the curve is efficient, points inside mean idle resources, and points outside are out of reach for now. A bowed-out PPC means increasing opportunity cost, a straight one constant cost. More resources or better technology shift the curve outward; moving resources from one good to the other is a movement along it.
comparative-advantage: Absolute advantage is producing more with the same resources; comparative advantage is producing at a lower opportunity cost. Find each country's opportunity cost of each good from output or input data, give each good to the country with the lower cost, and trade at terms between the two costs. Then both countries gain, and each can consume outside its own PPC, even if one has the absolute advantage in both goods.
demand: The law of demand says that as a good's price rises, the quantity demanded falls, other things equal, because of the income and substitution effects. A change in the good's own price moves buyers along the demand curve; a change in tastes, income, the prices of substitutes or complements, expectations or the number of buyers shifts the whole curve. Keep the words straight: quantity demanded for a movement, demand for a shift.
supply: The law of supply says that as a good's price rises, the quantity supplied rises, other things equal. A change in the good's own price moves sellers along the supply curve; a change in input costs, technology, taxes or subsidies, expectations or the number of sellers shifts the whole curve. Higher costs and taxes shift supply left; lower costs, better technology, subsidies and more sellers shift it right.
market-equilibrium: A market is in equilibrium where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Below that price a shortage pushes the price up, and above it a surplus pushes the price down, until the market clears. When one curve shifts, the equilibrium moves along the other: a demand shift moves price and quantity the same way, a supply shift moves them in opposite ways. When both curves shift, one of the two changes is indeterminate without the sizes of the shifts.
gdp-circular-flow: The circular flow shows households selling factors of production to firms and buying their output, so spending on final goods equals income. GDP is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country in a year, measured by C + I + G + (X − M) . Intermediate goods, used goods, financial trades and transfer payments are left out.
gdp-limitations: GDP measures market production, so it leaves out nonmarket activity such as home production, the underground economy, the value of leisure and environmental damage, and it can miss quality gains. To compare living standards, use GDP per capita (GDP divided by population), keeping in mind that an average hides how income is shared.
unemployment: The labor force is the employed plus the unemployed; the unemployment rate divides the unemployed by the labor force, and the participation rate divides the labor force by the adult population. Frictional and structural unemployment make up the natural rate; cyclical unemployment is the actual rate minus the natural rate. Discouraged and underemployed workers make the official rate understate joblessness.
price-indices-inflation: A price index compares the cost of a fixed basket with its cost in the base year (index 100). The consumer price index uses a basket households buy; the inflation rate is the percent change in the index. Dividing a nominal value by the index and multiplying by 100 gives a real value. Substitution bias, new goods and quality gains make the CPI overstate inflation.
inflation-costs: When inflation is higher than people anticipated, fixed-rate borrowers repay in dollars that buy less, so they gain while lenders, savers and people on fixed incomes lose; lower-than-anticipated inflation reverses this. Anticipated inflation is built into contracts. Any inflation brings menu costs and shoe-leather costs, and unpredictable inflation makes long-term planning harder.
real-nominal-gdp: Nominal GDP values output at current prices; real GDP values it at base-year prices, so only real GDP changes with production. The GDP deflator is nominal GDP divided by real GDP times 100, and real GDP is nominal GDP divided by the deflator times 100. The growth rate of real GDP is its percent change, and real GDP per capita measures living standards.
business-cycles: Real GDP rises in expansions and falls in contractions around potential output, the full-employment level that grows over time. The output gap is real GDP minus potential: a negative (recessionary) gap brings cyclical unemployment, and a positive (inflationary) gap brings unemployment below the natural rate and rising inflation. Peak and trough are the turning points between the phases.
aggregate-demand: Aggregate demand is total planned spending on real output at each price level, C + I + G + (X - M). It slopes down because a lower price level raises real wealth, lowers interest rates and makes domestic goods cheaper than foreign ones. A change in the price level moves along AD; a change in spending for any other reason shifts it.
multipliers: Each new dollar of spending becomes someone's income, who spends the MPC share of it, so output rises by a multiple of the first change. The spending multiplier is 1 / MPS; the tax multiplier is -MPC / MPS, one smaller in size because part of a tax cut is saved. To close a gap, choose the direction first, then divide the gap by the multiplier.
sras: SRAS shows the real output firms supply at each price level while wages and some prices are sticky, so it slopes up. A change in the price level moves along SRAS. Changes in input prices, productivity, taxes and rules on firms, or the wages workers bargain for, shift it: higher costs shift SRAS left, lower costs shift it right.
lras: In the long run, nominal wages and input prices catch up with the price level, so real output depends only on resources and technology. LRAS is vertical at full-employment output, and it shifts right when the economy gains labor, capital or better technology, just as the PPC shifts out. Spending and the price level do not move it.
adas-equilibrium: The AD-AS model shows the price level and real GDP where AD meets SRAS (short-run equilibrium). Comparing that output with LRAS shows the gap: left of LRAS is a recessionary gap with unemployment above the natural rate, right of LRAS an inflationary gap with unemployment below it. Long-run equilibrium is where all three curves meet.
adas-short-run-changes: In the short run, a shift of AD moves the price level and real GDP in the same direction (demand-pull inflation when AD rises), while a shift of SRAS moves them in opposite directions (cost-push inflation and stagflation when SRAS falls). Unemployment moves opposite to output. When both curves shift, one of the two outcomes is indeterminate.
long-run-self-adjustment: Left alone, an economy closes its own output gap through nominal wages and input prices. In a recessionary gap, high unemployment pushes wages down, SRAS shifts right, and output returns to full employment at a lower price level; in an inflationary gap, wages rise and SRAS shifts left, raising the price level. AD is not the mechanism, and in the long run AD changes only the price level.
fiscal-policy: Fiscal policy uses government purchases, taxes and transfers to shift aggregate demand. In a recessionary gap, expansionary policy (more G, lower taxes, more transfers) shifts AD right, raising output and the price level; in an inflationary gap, contractionary policy shifts AD left. Size it with the gap: direction first, then divide the gap by the spending or tax multiplier.
automatic-stabilizers: Automatic stabilizers are tax and transfer rules that respond to the business cycle by themselves. In a recession, progressive income taxes fall faster than income and unemployment compensation rises, so disposable income, consumption and AD fall by less; in a boom they slow AD's rise. They soften fluctuations quickly, but they do not close a gap and are not the self-adjustment mechanism.
financial-assets: Financial assets are claims on money or future income: money, bonds and stocks. A bond is a loan to its issuer and a stock is a share of ownership. Assets trade off liquidity, risk and return, and money is the most liquid. The interest rate is the price of borrowing. Because a bond pays a fixed amount, its price moves opposite to market interest rates.
nominal-real-rates: The nominal interest rate is the rate stated in dollars; the real interest rate is the gain in buying power, the nominal rate minus the expected inflation rate. Lenders add the expected inflation rate to the real return they want, so nominal rates rise when lenders expect more inflation. When inflation turns out higher than expected, fixed-rate borrowers gain and lenders lose, because the real rate actually paid falls.
money-functions: Money is whatever people accept as a medium of exchange, use as a unit of account and hold as a store of value. Modern money is fiat money, valued because the government declares it money and people accept it. M1 counts the most spendable money: currency held by the public and checkable deposits. M2 adds less liquid near-money, such as small time deposits and retail money market funds. Credit cards, stocks and bonds are not money.
banking-money-supply: Banks hold a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend the rest. Required reserves are deposits times the required reserve ratio, which the central bank sets, and excess reserves are the rest of a bank's reserves. A bank creates money when it lends its excess reserves, because the loan becomes a new deposit. As loans are spent and redeposited, the money supply can grow by up to excess reserves times the money multiplier, 1 / required reserve ratio, less when banks hold extra reserves or people hold cash.
money-market: The money market sets the nominal interest rate. Money demand slopes down because the nominal interest rate is the opportunity cost of holding money, and it shifts right when the price level or real GDP rises. The money supply is vertical, set by the central bank. A rise in money demand, or a fall in money supply, raises the nominal interest rate and lowers bond prices; a rise in money supply lowers the rate and raises bond prices.
monetary-policy: Monetary policy is the central bank changing interest rates to shift aggregate demand. With limited reserves, open market operations, the discount rate and the reserve requirement change the money supply, shown on the money market graph. With ample reserves, the Federal Reserve sets administered rates, mainly the interest on reserve balances; on the reserve market graph the flat part of reserve demand moves with them and the policy rate follows, while shifts in reserve supply leave the rate alone. Lower rates raise investment and interest-sensitive consumption, so AD rises; higher rates do the reverse.
loanable-funds: The loanable funds market brings together saving (supply) and borrowing (demand), and its price is the real interest rate. National saving is private saving plus public saving, and public saving is negative when the government spends more than it collects. More government borrowing shifts the demand for loanable funds right, raising the real interest rate and lowering private investment. More private saving shifts supply right, lowering the real interest rate and raising investment.
policy-short-run: In the short run, fiscal and monetary policy both work by shifting AD. Expansionary policy (more spending, lower taxes, a lower policy rate) closes a recessionary gap; contractionary policy closes an inflationary one. Each explanation names every link, states the reserves framework and its tool, and treats a policy mix carefully: when one variable is pushed two ways, its change is indeterminate.
phillips-curve: The short-run Phillips curve slopes down: changes in AD trade unemployment for inflation along it. Supply shocks and changes in expected inflation shift it. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment, matching LRAS, so in the long run unemployment returns to the natural rate and only inflation depends on what people expect.
money-growth-inflation: The quantity theory says M x V = P x Y. With velocity steady and real output fixed by resources and technology in the long run, the price level rises in proportion to the money supply, so sustained inflation comes from money growing faster than output. Money is neutral in the long run: it changes nominal variables, not real GDP or unemployment, although it can change output in the short run while wages are sticky.
deficits-debt: A budget deficit is one year's excess of government outlays over tax revenue; a surplus is the reverse. The government borrows to cover a deficit, so the national debt, a stock, rises by each deficit and falls only with a surplus. Expansionary fiscal policy and recessions widen deficits, contractionary policy and expansions narrow them, and interest on the debt is itself part of outlays.
crowding-out: When a government borrows to pay for a deficit, the demand for loanable funds rises and the real interest rate rises. Private investment and other interest-sensitive spending fall, offsetting part of the boost to AD. Year after year, lower investment means a smaller capital stock and slower growth of potential output. Crowding out is strongest near full employment and is eased by more private saving.
economic-growth: Long-run economic growth is a sustained rise in potential output and real GDP per capita. It comes from more physical capital, more human capital, better technology and more resources, all of which raise productivity. On the graphs, the PPC shifts out and LRAS shifts right. Living standards rise when output grows faster than population, and a choice of more capital goods today raises growth later.
growth-policy: Public policy can raise long-run growth by adding to physical capital, human capital, technology and infrastructure, or by strengthening incentives to work, save and invest (supply-side fiscal policy). Such policies aim at LRAS, though many also raise AD in the short run. Policies that only raise spending shift AD, and deficit-financed programs can lose part of their effect to crowding out.
balance-of-payments: The balance of payments has two halves. The current account records trade in goods and services, income and transfers; the capital and financial account records purchases and sales of assets. Because every purchase from abroad is paid for somehow, the two balances sum to zero: a current account deficit comes with a capital and financial account surplus of the same size. And a budget deficit is a different thing altogether.
exchange-rates: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another, and it can be written two ways that are reciprocals of each other. When one unit of a currency buys more of the other currency, it has appreciated, and the other has depreciated by the same change. Read the units before you compare two rates or convert a price: the units tell you which currency the number is the price of.
foreign-exchange-market: The foreign exchange market is a supply and demand market for a currency. Draw it with the quantity of the currency across the bottom and its price in the other currency per unit up the side. Foreigners buying the country's goods and assets demand its currency; its own residents buying foreign goods and assets supply it. The same trades show up as the mirror change in the market for the other currency, so when one currency appreciates, the other depreciates.
fx-policy-changes: A currency's value moves when its demand or supply shifts, and four shifters do most of the work: tastes, relative incomes, relative price levels and relative real interest rates, plus expectations. Higher real interest rates at home raise demand for the home currency, so it appreciates; higher inflation or faster income growth at home push it down. Policy acts through these: anything that raises a country's interest rates, such as contractionary monetary policy or more government borrowing, tends to make its currency appreciate. Always name the curve that shifts and say which way.
fx-net-exports: When a currency appreciates, everything the country sells costs foreign buyers more and everything it buys from abroad costs its residents less. Exports fall, imports rise and net exports fall, so aggregate demand shifts left and output and the price level fall in the short run. A depreciation works the other way round. Always state the link through net exports and AD, and remember that the trading partner sees the mirror change.
real-rates-financial-flows: Relative real interest rates steer financial capital between countries. When one country's real rate rises above others', savers abroad buy its assets: financial capital flows in, its capital and financial account balance rises, the demand for its currency rises and the currency appreciates, so its net exports and current account balance fall. The inflow also adds to its supply of loanable funds. Write the whole chain, link by link, and use the real interest rate.
